paper_metadata.title: Predicting recovery in patients with mild traumatic brain injury and a normal CT using serum biomarkers and diffusion tensor imaging (CENTER-TBI): an observational cohort study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a large, prospective, multi-center cohort (CENTER-TBI) with well-defined inclusion/exclusion criteria. The source population and recruitment methods are thoroughly described, and baseline characteristics are provided for both the biomarker and DTI sub-cohorts.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: We selected patients from the Collaborative European NeuroTrauma Effectiveness Research in Traumatic Brain Injury (CENTER-TBI) study... a prospective longitudinal multinational cohort study which recruited from 19th December 2014 to 17th December 2017 at centers in Europe and Israel.
items.reasoning: The study clearly identifies the source as the CENTER-TBI multinational cohort and specifies the recruitment timeframe and geographic scope.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria for the current analysis were GCS 13–15 on presentation and a normal acute CT.
items.reasoning: The recruitment is based on a standardized protocol across 15 sites with specific clinical criteria (GCS and CT status).

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: recruited between December 19, 2014 and December 17, 2017
items.reasoning: Specific dates for the recruitment period are provided.

items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described

items.reasoning: The geographic setting is explicitly stated as multi-center across Europe and Israel.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria for the current analysis were GCS 13–15 on presentation and a normal acute CT. For the analysis assessing the prognostic value of biomarkers patients must have been aged ≥ 18 years... For the analysis assessing the prognostic value of DTI, patients must have been aged 20–70 years
items.reasoning: Criteria are clearly defined, including clinical severity (GCS), imaging status (normal CT), and age ranges for specific sub-analyses.

items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Among 1025 patients with biomarkers, aged 18-93 (median 48), 656 (64%) male... MRI was available for 153 patients (aged 20–70 (median 44) years, 71% male)
items.reasoning: Key demographics (age, sex) and clinical status (GCS, CT) are provided for the analyzed samples.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition is well-managed. Outcome data was available for over 80% of the biomarker cohort and 97% of the DTI cohort. Missing data was handled using multiple imputation, and sensitivity analyses (best/worst case) were performed to ensure robustness.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Outcome data were missing in <18% and <3% of patients in the larger serum biomarker and smaller DTI cohorts, respectively.
items.reasoning: The follow-up rate for the primary outcome (GOSE at 3 months) is high, particularly in the DTI cohort.

items.evidence_snippet: supported by the patients with and without missing data being similar in the most characteristics except for educational level which tended to be higher in patients with complete data (Supplementary Table S1).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors (biomarkers and DTI) were measured using standardized, high-quality protocols. DTI data underwent sophisticated harmonization (ComBat) and age-correction to ensure reliability across different centers and age groups.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Biomarkers (GFAP, NFL, S100B) were obtained at a median of 8.8 h... DTI metrics were available in 153 patients for 48 white matter tracts (ICBM-DTI-81 atlas).
items.reasoning: The PFs are clearly defined as specific serum proteins and DTI metrics (FA/MD) across specific anatomical tracts.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Analysis for S100B was performed... using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay kit... Analysis for GFAP and NFL occurred... using a Single Molecule Arrays (SiMoA) based assay... DTI was acquired on 17 different 3.0 T machines... pre-agreed and included 32 directions
items.reasoning: The study used high-sensitivity assays (SiMoA) and standardized MRI protocols across sites.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: The FA and MD values were age-corrected... centred and scaled (i.e., z-scored).
items.reasoning: DTI metrics were treated as continuous variables. Biomarker cut-points were explored in a separate triage analysis but the main prognostic models used continuous data.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: DTI protocols across CENTER-TBI were pre-agreed... DTI was acquired on 17 different 3.0 T machines across 15 sites... harmonized using the Combat algorithm
items.reasoning: While multiple scanners were used, protocols were standardized and statistical harmonization was applied to minimize site-related variance.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Missing data for acute variables ranged from 0–17% to 0–12%, respectively.
items.reasoning: The amount of missing data for the primary prognostic factors was relatively low and handled via imputation.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Missing data was handled under the missing at random (MAR) assumption using multiple imputation as implemented in the R mice package.
items.reasoning: Multiple imputation is a standard and appropriate method for handling missing prognostic data.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (GOSE) is a standard, validated measure in TBI research. It was assessed at a consistent time point (3 months) and dichotomized appropriately. Centralized reading/curation was used to ensure consistency.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Outcome was assessed at 3 months (76–125 days) using the extended Glasgow Outcome Score (GOSE) which was dichotomized into complete recovery (GOSE = 8) and incomplete recovery (GOSE <8).
items.reasoning: The outcome, its timing, and the threshold for 'incomplete recovery' are explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: The GOSE is commonly used as the primary outcome measure in TBI studies... Missing values for GOSE were centrally imputed by the CENTER-TBI data curation team
items.reasoning: GOSE is the gold standard in the field, and centralized curation reduces inter-site variability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Outcome was assessed at 3 months (76–125 days) using the extended Glasgow Outcome Score (GOSE)
items.reasoning: A standardized assessment tool and timeframe were applied to all participants.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study rigorously accounts for confounding by using established clinical reference models (UPFRONT, HeadSMART, CENTER-TBI) as the baseline. The incremental value of biomarkers/DTI was tested by adding them to these multivariable models, ensuring that the effects were not simply due to age, sex, or injury severity.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1: Existing models... Age, Sex, Education level, Prior mental health problems, Alcohol intoxication, GCS, PTA, ISS, Mechanism of injury
items.reasoning: The study includes a comprehensive list of known clinical and demographic confounders used in validated TBI models.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 summarizes these five existing prognostic models using clinical variables... GCS, Glasgow Coma Score; PTA, Post-traumatic amnesia; ASA level, American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status; ISS, Injury severity score.
items.reasoning: Standard clinical definitions and scales were used for all confounding variables.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical data was accessed via the Neurobot platform (RRID/SCR_017004, core data, version 3.0).
items.reasoning: Data was sourced from a high-quality, curated database (Neurobot) using standardized Common Data Elements.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical data was accessed via the Neurobot platform
items.reasoning: Standardized data collection protocols were used across all CENTER-TBI sites.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Missing data was handled under the missing at random (MAR) assumption using multiple imputation as implemented in the R mice package.
items.reasoning: Multiple imputation was applied to all variables in the models, including confounders.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: The control cohort consisted of 157 healthy volunteers who were scanned using the same scanners and imaging protocols as the patients.
items.reasoning: While the study didn't match patients, it used a healthy control group to establish age-correction 'detrending' for DTI metrics.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: To understand if serum biomarkers/DTI could improve the reference models, we fitted the reference models with and without the serum biomarkers/DTI score.
items.reasoning: The primary analysis was based on multivariable adjustment using established clinical models, which is the correct approach for assessing incremental prognostic value.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical analysis is highly robust, following TRIPOD guidelines. It uses appropriate techniques for variable selection (Lasso), model comparison (Likelihood ratio tests), and internal validation (bootstrapping). The reporting is transparent, including calibration plots and optimism-corrected metrics.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Statistical analysis was conducted in R 4.3.1... The statistical code is freely available at https://github.com/DrSophieRichter/DTImTBI.
items.reasoning: The methods are detailed, and the provision of open-source code allows for full reproducibility.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: To identify the most prognostic of the 48 white matter tracts we used lasso logistic regression... To understand if serum biomarkers/DTI could improve the reference models, we fitted the reference models with and without the serum biomarkers/DTI score.
items.reasoning: The study uses a logical two-step approach: identifying the best DTI predictors via Lasso, then testing their incremental value over established clinical models.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Model performance was measured using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), the Cox calibration intercept and a slope, the Nagelkerke R2... internal validation... using 200 bootstrap samples
items.reasoning: The use of AUC, R2, and bootstrapping for internal validation is the standard of excellence for prognosis studies.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Results were reported as per TRIPOD for prognostic studies.
items.reasoning: The authors report all pre-specified outcomes, including negative results for biomarkers, and provide comprehensive performance metrics.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
